subtype: Approach: paying savings first through automation [Action]
passage: Shreya's salary arrived on the last day of the month, and by the fifth it had always vanished. This time she had set up two standing instructions the week before: a fixed amount to her savings account, and a smaller fixed amount into a monthly investment plan, both due to leave within an hour of the salary landing, before she could see the balance and feel generous. The month was tight; her flatmate Urmila's birthday and a phone repair meant less to play with. "You'll run out by the twentieth," Urmila said. Shreya shrugged. "Then I'll spend less. The savings are already gone. I can't argue with them." On the twentieth she had a little left, and the savings account had grown for the first time in a year without a single decision.

qa.q: What did Shreya set up in the week before her salary arrived?
qa.a: She set up two standing instructions: a fixed amount to her savings account and a smaller fixed amount into a monthly investment plan.

qa.q: What does Shreya's shrug and "I can't argue with them" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Shreya feels calm and settled about the plan, because the savings leave before she can be tempted.

qa.q: What other approach could Shreya add to this one?
qa.a: She could give each spending category an amount, or note where the leftover money goes, so the rest of the month is planned too.

qa.q: How might Urmila see the plan?
qa.a: Urmila seems doubtful that what is left will last until the end of the month, though the plan does not depend on willpower.

grounding: Shreya automates a fixed amount to savings and a monthly investment plan right after salary arrives, so saving is the default.

subtype: Approach: prioritising debts by interest rate [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday. Imran and Nilesh spread their statements on the table: an education loan with a much lower interest rate, and a credit card with money still owed. "Which one costs us more each month?" Nilesh asked. Imran circled the two rates.

Friday. "The card's rate is far higher than the loan's," Imran said. "So every spare rupee goes to the card, and the loan just gets its minimum." Nilesh hesitated. "It feels wrong not to pay everything down evenly." "Evenly is comfortable," said Imran. "The order is what counts."

Sunday, three weeks later. The card balance was down to a tenth of what it had been. Nilesh set a reminder to pay the loan's minimum on the same day every month and otherwise left the loan alone. "I didn't think ordering things would feel so much like progress."

qa.q: Where did Imran and Nilesh send every spare rupee?
qa.a: Every spare rupee went to the card.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when Imran suggested not paying everything down evenly?
qa.a: Nilesh felt hesitant and uneasy, since it felt wrong not to pay everything down evenly.

qa.q: What could they do if they are unsure this order suits their own situation?
qa.a: They could ask the bank or a qualified adviser to check their figures, since loan terms differ.

qa.q: How does Imran see paying down every debt evenly?
qa.a: Imran sees it as comfortable but less useful than choosing the order carefully.

grounding: Imran and Nilesh look at the interest on a card and a loan, put extra money on the card first and pay only the minimum on the loan.

passage:
Sunaina: The insurance renewal notice came. Due next month.
Hrithik: Again?? That wrecked our March last time.
Sunaina: And Diwali. And the geyser repair in June. Every year the same three things blow up the budget.
Hrithik: They're not really surprises though. We just forget they're yearly.
Sunaina: What if we put a little aside every month for exactly those? Insurance, festivals, repairs. Its own pot.
Hrithik: So when the bill comes the money's already there.
Sunaina: Not an emergency. Just a Tuesday.
Hrithik: Love it. Start this month? 🙂
Sunaina: Starting today 🙂

qa.q: Which three yearly costs did Sunaina name?
qa.a: The insurance renewal, Diwali and the geyser repair in June.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's "Again??" suggest about how Hrithik feels?
qa.a: It suggests Hrithik feels frustrated and a little dreading the bill, remembering how it wrecked March.

qa.q: What other approach could help them set the right amount for the pot?
qa.a: They could look at last year's statements to see what each yearly cost really was and spread that over the twelve months.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt about the yearly bills before the idea?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt stressed by the same three costs upsetting the budget every year, which is why the idea came quickly.

grounding: Sunaina and Hrithik notice yearly costs like insurance, festivals and repairs upset monthly plans, so they put a little aside each month.

subtype: Approach: strict budgeting that collapses in month three [Pitfall]
passage: In the market lane of a small hill town, Darshan and Ankita began the new budget with a hopeful chart on the fridge: every rupee named, no eating out, no cinema, not even chai at the stall. For ten weeks it worked. Ankita counted coins into a tin. Then one Sunday, walking back from the bus, Darshan stopped at the snack cart and bought two plates of momos. "It's just one plate," said Darshan. "And one for me," said Ankita, and they ate them on a wall, guilty and happy. By evening the chart looked wrong. "We've broken it," said Ankita. "So what's the point?" By the third month the chart was in a drawer, and they were spending as freely as before, only now it felt like failing.

qa.q: What did Darshan buy at the snack cart?
qa.a: Darshan bought two plates of momos.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when saying "We've broken it"?
qa.a: Ankita felt guilty and discouraged, as though the whole plan had failed.

qa.q: What could they do differently next time?
qa.a: They could include a small amount of fun money so a treat fits inside the plan, and treat a slip as something to adjust rather than a reason to quit.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel after the chart went into the drawer?
qa.a: Darshan may feel responsible for starting the slip, though the treat was also the one bright moment in a very tight plan.

grounding: Darshan and Ankita follow a very tight plan with no fun money, one outing breaks it, and they abandon the budget.

passage:
Sahil: Account's nearly empty and it's only the 26th??
Tanvir: How? Rent, groceries and the phone bill are all paid. Nothing big happened.
Sahil: I checked. No big charges at all.
Tanvir: The office snacks, the late-night orders, the cab when it rained...
Sahil: Those are like a hundred rupees each. That's nothing.
Tanvir: Maybe nothing times forty is something.
Sahil: I never wrote any of it down.
Tanvir: Neither did I. Each one felt too small to count.
Sahil: So where did it go?
Tanvir: I honestly don't know. I never counted them.
Sahil: Same. 😕

qa.q: What day of the month is it when Sahil notices the account is nearly empty?
qa.a: It is the 26th.

qa.q: What does Sahil's "??" after the 26th suggest about how Sahil feels?
qa.a: It suggests Sahil feels shocked and worried, since nothing big seems to explain the empty account.

qa.q: What could they do to find out where the money goes?
qa.a: For a few weeks they could note every purchase, even the small ones, to see what adds up.

qa.q: How might Tanvir be feeling as the conversation ends?
qa.a: Tanvir seems puzzled and a little guilty, since neither of them counted the small things.

grounding: Sahil and Tanvir never count small daily purchases, and at month end the account is short and neither can say where the money went.

subtype: Approach: revising categories after an income change [Revision]
passage: When Omkar's raise arrived, the first thing Jasleen noticed was how fast the ideas came: a bigger flat, a new car, a holiday abroad. A showroom in town had an offer ending on Saturday, which made everything feel urgent. "Let's not touch the spending plan tonight," said Jasleen. "Let's sleep on it and rewrite it on Sunday." They sat down with the old sheet after the offer had expired. The extra money went into three parts: a higher amount to savings, a small upgrade to their own life, and a fund for sending money to Omkar's parents every month. "The upgrade first is a better mattress," Jasleen said, laughing, and wrote it down. The car offer passed. Neither of them missed it.

qa.q: What were the three parts the extra income was split into?
qa.a: A higher amount to savings, a small upgrade to their own life, and a fund for sending money to Omkar's parents.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling about the showroom's deadline?
qa.a: Jasleen was wary of the false urgency and wanted to stay calm, choosing to sleep on it first.

qa.q: What could they do if Omkar's parents' needs change later?
qa.a: They could review the size of the fund as part of the monthly plan and change it together.

qa.q: How might Omkar's parents see the new fund?
qa.a: They may feel grateful and relieved, and perhaps a little uneasy about receiving money.

grounding: After a raise, Jasleen and Omkar resist raising spending, split it into savings, a small upgrade and a parents' fund, and rewrite the plan.

subtype: Approach: separate accounts for shared bills and personal spending [Action]
passage: Every first of the month, Avni and Abhinav each moved money into their joint account, in proportion to what each earned: Abhinav's share bigger, Avni's smaller. That one account paid the rent, the groceries and the home-loan instalments. Whatever stayed in their own accounts was theirs to spend without explanation. It had begun after an argument about a pair of headphones. Now Abhinav bought comics without a word, and Avni paid for art classes and never had to justify the fees. On a Saturday in Pune, Abhinav came home with a new board game and Avni looked up from the sofa. "Did you check the budget?" "It's my money," said Abhinav, grinning. Avni just smiled. "Have fun." The old friction had gone.

qa.q: What did the joint account pay for?
qa.a: The rent, the groceries and the home-loan instalments.

qa.q: What does Avni's smile and "Have fun" suggest about how Avni feels?
qa.a: It suggests Avni feels relaxed and content, since personal spending no longer needs a defence.

qa.q: What could they do if one of their incomes changes?
qa.a: They could work out the shares again in proportion to income so the joint account stays fair.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel about not having spending checked?
qa.a: Abhinav likely feels free and respected, and grins about it.

grounding: Avni and Abhinav keep a joint account for rent, groceries and loan instalments funded in proportion to income and spend the rest freely.

subtype: Approach: cutting losses on an unused commitment [Revision]
passage: We were going through last quarter's bank statements one evening, me with a highlighter and Siddharth with a bowl of roasted chana, when I found three lines that made me stop. Membership at a gym, and two video subscriptions. Nobody in the flat had used any of them since spring. I'm Ankita, by the way. My first thought was, but we paid for the whole year of the gym! It felt like throwing away the money already spent. Siddharth said, "That money's gone either way. The only question is whether we keep paying." So we cancelled all three that same night. The monthly amount went into a small travel fund, and I checked it last week: enough for a long weekend in the hills. I still wince about the gym, but less than the monthly wince.

qa.q: Where did the money from the cancelled plans go?
qa.a: It went into a small travel fund.

qa.q: What did Ankita feel when first seeing the gym charge?
qa.a: Ankita felt reluctant to let go, since cancelling seemed like throwing away money already spent.

qa.q: What could Ankita and Siddharth do to catch this earlier?
qa.a: They could go through their statements every few months and cancel anything nobody uses.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the money already spent?
qa.a: Siddharth sees it as gone either way, so the only question is whether to keep paying.

grounding: Ankita and Siddharth find a gym and two video plans nobody uses, cancel them despite the money already spent and redirect the amount to a travel fund.

subtype: Approach: gathering documents and understanding the facts [Thinking]
passage: Before the family meeting in Bhawani village, Neelam spent two evenings going through the tin trunk in the storeroom. She laid the papers out on the cot: the old land record, a receipt for the house tax, a letter from the panchayat. She read the names slowly and noted who was written where. Then she rang her brother Amandeep and an aunt and asked each what they believed was true. Amandeep said the house was obviously meant for the eldest. The aunt said their father had promised her the front room. Neelam wrote each belief in a notebook beside the papers without arguing. By the time they met, she knew what the papers said and what people believed, and they were not always the same. She did not say who was right. She said, "Let's start with what's written."

qa.q: Where did Neelam find the papers?
qa.a: She found them in the tin trunk in the storeroom.

qa.q: What might Neelam be feeling as she avoids arguing with Amandeep and the aunt?
qa.a: Neelam is probably feeling careful and wary, wanting to keep the peace while she learns what each person believes.

qa.q: What could Neelam do next?
qa.a: Neelam could share her notes with everyone and suggest a neutral helper, keeping the talk on what the papers show.

qa.q: How might the aunt feel if the papers do not match what their father promised?
qa.a: The aunt may feel hurt or uncertain, since the promise she remembers might not be written down.

grounding: Before the family talk about the ancestral house, Neelam collects the papers, checks the names on them and notes what each relative assumes.

subtype: Approach: consulting a lawyer for general guidance [Action]
passage:
'We don't know the rules,' said Bidisha. 'Half of what Papa's cousin tells us contradicts the other half.'
'Then let's ask,' said Tushar. 'A lawyer, one meeting, just to explain in general what the options are.'
'Not to fight?'
'No. I don't want a letter in anyone's hand. I want to understand.'
Two days later, at the kitchen table:
'The lawyer said there are ways to settle by agreement, and listed them,' said Bidisha, reading from her notes.
'And what was said about the house is general, not our exact case.'
'Right. So we don't wave it at Chachi.'
'We bring it to the table and ask: here are the options, which one works for all of us?'
Tushar closed the notebook. 'Sunday, then. Tea first, papers second.'

qa.q: What did the siblings ask the lawyer for?
qa.a: They asked for one meeting, just to explain in general what the options are.

qa.q: What does Tushar's line "I don't want a letter in anyone's hand" suggest about how Tushar feels?
qa.a: It suggests Tushar wants peace and fears that a legal letter would escalate the dispute.

qa.q: What could the siblings do if the family still disagrees on Sunday?
qa.a: They could go through the options one by one and, if needed, ask the lawyer again about their exact case, while keeping the mood calm.

qa.q: How might Chachi feel if the lawyer's words were used against Chachi?
qa.a: Chachi might feel attacked and defensive, which is why the siblings decide to offer options rather than wave the advice.

grounding: Bidisha and Tushar ask a lawyer to explain the general position and settlement options, and plan to use it to frame talk, not as a weapon.
